cards.question_text: What are the six steps of the NIST SP 800-61 incident response lifecycle, in order?
choices: Preparation → Detection & Analysis → Containment, Eradication & Recovery → Post-Incident Activity
Detection → Containment → Eradication → Recovery → Reporting → Closure
Identification → Triage → Remediation → Forensics → Reporting → Lessons Learned
Prevent → Detect → Respond → Recover → Report → Retire
cards.answer: Preparation → Detection & Analysis → Containment, Eradication & Recovery → Post-Incident Activity
cards.explanation_correct: NIST SP 800-61 defines four phases: (1) Preparation — building toolkits, training teams, establishing policies and communication channels before an incident. (2) Detection & Analysis — identifying incidents from alerts, logs, SIEM, or user reports, then triaging and analyzing scope. (3) Containment, Eradication & Recovery — stopping the spread (isolate hosts, block IPs), removing the threat (delete malware, close vulnerabilities), and restoring systems to normal operation. (4) Post-Incident Activity — lessons learned, documentation, process improvement. The list in Option A covers all four phases (phase 3 has three sub-steps). Preparation is the most important phase because it's the only one you control before an incident occurs.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Option B is a simplified ad-hoc list, not NIST's structured lifecycle. Option C uses different terminology (Triage, Remediation, Forensics) that doesn't match NIST SP 800-61 phases. Option D (Prevent, Detect, Respond, Recover, Report, Retire) is not a recognized IR framework — it resembles generic risk management cycles.

cards.question_text: What is the single most important phase of incident response, and why?
choices: Preparation — it is the only phase performed before an incident occurs, and it determines how effectively all other phases execute
Detection — because finding the incident first is harder than fixing it
Recovery — because restoring service is what the business ultimately cares about
Post-Incident Activity — because lessons learned prevent all future incidents
cards.answer: Preparation — it is the only phase performed before an incident occurs, and it determines how effectively all other phases execute
cards.explanation_correct: Preparation is foundational: establishing IR policies, training the response team, building contact lists, pre-deploying forensic toolkits, configuring logging and alerting, setting up communication channels (out-of-band if email is compromised), defining escalation thresholds, and running tabletop exercises. Without preparation, teams scramble during an actual incident — wasting critical time, making mistakes, and missing evidence. A well-prepared team can execute containment in minutes instead of hours. Tabletop exercises (simulated incident walk-throughs) during preparation expose gaps before they matter. Preparation is the phase you fully control; once an incident starts, you're reactive.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Option B is wrong — detection is critical but relies on preparation (logging, SIEM rules, alerting). Option C is wrong — recovery is important but depends on clean containment and eradication first. Option D is wrong — lessons learned improve future response but don't prevent ALL future incidents; new threats always emerge.

cards.question_text: A SOC analyst detects unusual outbound traffic from a web server at 2 AM. The server is sending 500MB/s to an unknown IP address. What should be the FIRST action in the incident response process?
choices: Follow the pre-established IR plan: verify the alert is a true positive (correlate with other logs/SIEM), then escalate to the IR team lead who authorizes containment — do not immediately power off the server
Immediately shut down the server to stop the data exfiltration and preserve evidence
Immediately block the destination IP on the firewall and continue business as usual
Call the police and report a cybersecurity crime before doing anything else
cards.answer: Follow the pre-established IR plan: verify the alert is a true positive (correlate with other logs/SIEM), then escalate to the IR team lead who authorizes containment — do not immediately power off the server
cards.explanation_correct: The first step in NIST's Detection & Analysis phase is to verify the incident is real (true positive vs false positive). This means correlating the alert with SIEM data, checking other logs, and confirming scope before acting. Premature actions — like shutting down the server — destroy volatile evidence (RAM contents, network connections, running processes) that are critical for forensics. Powering off can also trigger anti-forensic measures in malware (e.g., deleting itself on shutdown). The correct flow is: verify → escalate per IR plan → get authorization → contain strategically (network isolation, not power-off). Containment decisions should follow the plan, not be improvised.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Option B (immediate shutdown) is a classic mistake — it destroys volatile evidence (RAM, network state, running processes) and may trigger malware anti-forensic cleanup. Option C (block IP only) addresses the symptom but not the root cause — the server is compromised and needs full investigation. Option D (call police first) is premature — internal IR handles initial response; law enforcement is engaged later if warranted.

cards.question_text: During a ransomware incident, the IR team is debating between short-term containment (isolate infected hosts from the network) and long-term containment (rebuild systems from clean images). What is the correct sequencing?
choices: Short-term containment first (immediately isolate infected hosts to stop lateral spread), then proceed to eradication and recovery (rebuild from clean images), then long-term containment becomes part of recovery
Long-term containment first — immediately rebuild all systems to ensure they're clean, then isolate what's left
Skip containment entirely and go straight to eradication — delete the ransomware and decrypt files
Containment is optional — if you have good backups, just restore everything immediately without isolating anything
cards.answer: Short-term containment first (immediately isolate infected hosts to stop lateral spread), then proceed to eradication and recovery (rebuild from clean images), then long-term containment becomes part of recovery
cards.explanation_correct: NIST recommends short-term containment immediately — isolate infected hosts (network segmentation, disable accounts, block C2 traffic) to prevent the ransomware from spreading to other systems. This buys time for proper investigation. Long-term containment (rebuilding from clean images, applying patches, hardening) happens during the eradication and recovery phases. The sequence matters: if you try to rebuild while the threat is still active, the ransomware will re-infect the rebuilt systems. Containment must precede eradication. Short-term containment is a tactical emergency action; long-term containment is strategic and deliberate.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Option B is backwards — you can't rebuild while the threat is active (reinfection risk). Option C is wrong — containment is mandatory, not optional; without it the ransomware keeps spreading during eradication. Option D is dangerous — restoring from backups while the threat is active means the ransomware encrypts the restored data too.

cards.question_text: After containing a phishing campaign that compromised several employee accounts, the IR team moves to eradication. Which actions are part of the eradication phase?
choices: Disable compromised accounts, remove malicious mailbox rules the attackers created, delete phishing emails from all mailboxes, patch the vulnerability (e.g., MFA bypass), and remove any backdoor accounts or malware planted by the attackers
Restore email service from backup and send a company-wide notification that the incident is over
Conduct forensic disk imaging on all compromised machines and write a formal incident report
Interview each phishing victim about what they clicked and file an HR complaint against them
cards.answer: Disable compromised accounts, remove malicious mailbox rules the attackers created, delete phishing emails from all mailboxes, patch the vulnerability (e.g., MFA bypass), and remove any backdoor accounts or malware planted by the attackers
cards.explanation_correct: Eradication is about removing the root cause and all traces of the threat. In a phishing campaign: (1) Disable compromised accounts to stop attacker access. (2) Remove malicious mailbox rules — attackers often create forwarding rules (e.g., 'forward all emails with 'invoice' to external@evil.com') that persist even after password resets. Missing these means the attacker continues receiving data. (3) Purge phishing emails from all mailboxes to prevent re-clicking. (4) Patch the vulnerability that enabled the attack (if it was a technical exploit, not just social engineering). (5) Remove any backdoor accounts or persistent malware. Eradication must be thorough — any leftover artifact can lead to re-infection.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Option B describes recovery and notification, not eradication — the threat isn't removed, just restored around. Option C describes forensic collection and reporting — these happen in parallel but aren't eradication actions. Option D is an HR process — while user awareness matters, blaming victims is counterproductive and doesn't eradicate the threat.

cards.question_text: What is an Indicator of Compromise (IoC), and how does it differ from a regular log entry?
choices: An IoC is a forensic artifact (file hash, IP address, domain, registry key, behavioral pattern) that with high confidence indicates a system has been compromised or an attack is in progress — a regular log entry is just a record of activity, not necessarily malicious
An IoC is any error message in a system log, and a log entry is any informational message
An IoC is a type of antivirus signature, and a log entry is a firewall rule
An IoC is a legal document proving a breach occurred, while a log entry is an IT ticket
cards.answer: An IoC is a forensic artifact (file hash, IP address, domain, registry key, behavioral pattern) that with high confidence indicates a system has been compromised or an attack is in progress — a regular log entry is just a record of activity, not necessarily malicious
cards.explanation_correct: IoCs are specific, actionable artifacts that signal compromise. Common IoC types: file hashes (MD5/SHA256 of known malware), network indicators (C2 server IPs, suspicious domains, anomalous DNS queries), host indicators (unexpected registry modifications, new scheduled tasks, unauthorized service installations), and behavioral indicators (beaconing patterns, data exfiltration volume, lateral movement). A log entry (e.g., 'user jsmith logged in at 9:00 AM') is neutral data. An IoC transforms that data into a threat signal (e.g., 'user jsmith logged in from Russia at 3:00 AM — impossible travel IoC'). IoCs are shared via threat intelligence platforms (MISP, STIX/TAXII) and fed into SIEM/EDR for automated detection.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Option B is wrong — not all error messages are IoCs; IoCs require context and correlation. Option C is wrong — IoCs are broader than AV signatures (they include network and behavioral indicators). Option D is wrong — IoCs are technical artifacts, not legal documents.

cards.question_text: What is the difference between an IoC (Indicator of Compromise) and an IoA (Indicator of Attack)?
choices: IoCs are forensic artifacts found AFTER a compromise (reactive — evidence the attack succeeded), while IoAs are behaviors and techniques observed DURING an attack (proactive — evidence the attack is happening now, before damage is done)
IoCs are for malware and IoAs are for network attacks
IoCs are generated by SIEM and IoAs are generated by firewalls
There is no difference — they are two names for the same thing
cards.answer: IoCs are forensic artifacts found AFTER a compromise (reactive — evidence the attack succeeded), while IoAs are behaviors and techniques observed DURING an attack (proactive — evidence the attack is happening now, before damage is done)
cards.explanation_correct: IoCs (Indicator of Compromise) are post-incident artifacts: a malware hash on disk, a C2 IP in firewall logs, a modified registry key. They tell you 'this system was compromised.' IoAs (Indicator of Attack) are real-time behaviors: PowerShell executing encoded commands, a process injecting into another process, credential dumping via LSASS access, anomalous SMB lateral movement. IoAs tell you 'an attack is actively in progress.' IoAs map to MITRE ATT&CK techniques and are behavior-based — they catch novel attacks that don't have known IoCs (zero-days). IoCs are static (hashes, IPs) and can be evaded; IoAs focus on what the attacker is DOING, which is harder to disguise. Modern EDR/XDR platforms increasingly emphasize IoA detection.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Option B is wrong — both apply to any attack vector. Option C is wrong — both can be detected by various tools (SIEM, EDR, NDR). Option D is wrong — the distinction matters: IoCs are reactive (after), IoAs are proactive (during).

cards.question_text: A security analyst reviews a workstation and finds the following: a scheduled task named 'SystemUpdate' running PowerShell with an encoded command every 30 minutes, outbound connections to an IP in a country where the company has no business, and a new service binary in C:\\Temp\\. Which combination of these represents behavioral IoCs?
choices: The PowerShell encoded command execution (living-off-the-land technique), the periodic scheduled task (beaconing pattern), and the outbound connection to an unexpected geo — all are behavioral IoCs indicating active compromise
Only the IP address is an IoC — IPs are the only true indicators of compromise
Only the file in C:\\Temp\\ is an IoC — unexpected file locations are the sole indicator
None of these are IoCs unless the antivirus software flags them as malicious
cards.answer: The PowerShell encoded command execution (living-off-the-land technique), the periodic scheduled task (beaconing pattern), and the outbound connection to an unexpected geo — all are behavioral IoCs indicating active compromise
cards.explanation_correct: All three artifacts are behavioral IoCs: (1) PowerShell with -EncodedCommand is a classic living-off-the-land (LotL) technique — attackers use legitimate system tools to avoid detection. Encoded commands hide the payload from casual inspection. (2) A scheduled task running every 30 minutes suggests beaconing — malware checking in with C2 at regular intervals. (3) Outbound connections to unexpected geolocations are a network behavioral IoC. The file in C:\Temp\ is a static IoC (file artifact), not behavioral. Together, these form a kill chain: persistence (scheduled task) → execution (PowerShell) → C2 (outbound connection). This pattern maps to MITRE ATT&CK techniques T1053 (Scheduled Task), T1059 (PowerShell), T1071 (Application Layer Protocol).
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Option B is wrong — IPs are just one IoC type; behavioral indicators are equally or more important. Option C is wrong — file location is one indicator but ignoring behavioral patterns misses the full picture. Option D is wrong — IoCs are independent of AV detection; many sophisticated attacks evade AV but leave behavioral traces.

cards.question_text: Your SIEM generates an alert: a user account that normally logs in from Singapore at 9 AM just authenticated from an IP in Eastern Europe at 3 AM local time, then immediately attempted to download the entire customer database via a bulk export API. Which framework would best help classify what stage of attack this represents?
choices: MITRE ATT&CK — it maps the observed techniques (anomalous login = Initial Access/Credential Access; bulk data export = Exfiltration) to specific tactics and techniques, helping the IR team understand the attack stage and predict next steps
ISO 27001 — it provides the compliance checklist for reporting the breach to regulators
COBIT — it defines IT governance frameworks for database access policies
ITIL — it provides the incident management ticketing framework for the helpdesk
cards.answer: MITRE ATT&CK — it maps the observed techniques (anomalous login = Initial Access/Credential Access; bulk data export = Exfiltration) to specific tactics and techniques, helping the IR team understand the attack stage and predict next steps
cards.explanation_correct: MITRE ATT&CK is the industry-standard framework for classifying adversary behaviors. It organizes attacks into Tactics (the 'why' — what the attacker is trying to achieve) and Techniques (the 'how' — specific methods). This scenario maps to: Initial Access (T1078 — Valid Accounts, the compromised credentials), Collection (T1005 — Data from Local System, gathering the database), and Exfiltration (T1041 — Exfiltration Over C2 Channel or T1567 — Exfiltration Over Web Service). By mapping IoCs/IoAs to ATT&CK, the IR team understands the attack stage (here: late stage — exfiltration), predicts what the attacker might do next, and can prioritize containment of the highest-risk actions. ATT&CK also helps with threat hunting by identifying gaps in detection coverage.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Option B (ISO 27001) is a compliance standard, not an attack classification framework. Option C (COBIT) is IT governance, not threat behavior mapping. Option D (ITIL) is service management — useful for ticketing but doesn't classify attack stages.

cards.question_text: What is the 'order of volatility' in digital forensics, and why does it matter?
choices: It is the sequence in which evidence should be collected, starting from the most volatile (RAM, CPU cache, network connections) to the least volatile (hard drives, optical media) — because volatile data is lost when power is removed and must be captured first
It is the order in which forensic tools should be run: antivirus first, then disk imaging, then memory dump
It is the ranking of how dangerous a piece of evidence is to the investigator's safety
It is the order in which suspects should be interviewed based on how nervous they appear
cards.answer: It is the sequence in which evidence should be collected, starting from the most volatile (RAM, CPU cache, network connections) to the least volatile (hard drives, optical media) — because volatile data is lost when power is removed and must be captured first
cards.explanation_correct: The order of volatility (from RFC 3227) guides forensic collection priority: (1) CPU cache/registers — lost in milliseconds. (2) RAM — lost on power-off; contains running processes, network connections, encryption keys, decrypted data in memory. (3) Network state (connections, routing tables, ARP cache) — changes rapidly. (4) Running processes — terminate on shutdown. (5) Temporary files/swap — may be overwritten. (6) Hard drives — persistent but can be modified by malware. (7) Remote logs — persistent on log servers. (8) Physical configuration, network topology — least volatile. Collecting in this order ensures the most easily-lost evidence is captured before it disappears. RAM capture is critical — it can reveal decrypted files, in-memory malware, and active network connections that disk forensics cannot find.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Option B is wrong — the order of volatility is about evidence types, not tool sequencing. Option C is wrong — volatility refers to data persistence, not physical danger. Option D is wrong — it has nothing to do with interviewing suspects.

cards.question_text: What is a forensic hash, and why are TWO different hash algorithms (e.g., MD5 and SHA-256) sometimes computed for the same evidence?
choices: A forensic hash is a fixed-size fingerprint of data used to prove integrity. Two algorithms are used for redundancy — if a collision is found in one algorithm (like MD5's known weaknesses), the other (SHA-256) still verifies the evidence hasn't been tampered with
A forensic hash is a type of encryption that protects evidence from being read by unauthorized parties
A forensic hash is a timestamp applied to evidence to prove when it was collected
A forensic hash is a digital signature that proves who collected the evidence
cards.answer: A forensic hash is a fixed-size fingerprint of data used to prove integrity. Two algorithms are used for redundancy — if a collision is found in one algorithm (like MD5's known weaknesses), the other (SHA-256) still verifies the evidence hasn't been tampered with
cards.explanation_correct: A forensic hash (MD5, SHA-256, SHA-512) creates a unique fingerprint of data. If even one bit changes, the hash changes completely. In forensics, you hash evidence at collection time and again at analysis/presentation time — if the hashes match, the evidence is proven unaltered (integrity). Two algorithms provide defense-in-depth: MD5 has known collision vulnerabilities (two different inputs can produce the same hash), so using SHA-256 alongside it means even if MD5 is challenged in court, SHA-256 provides independent verification. The hash doesn't prove authenticity (who created it) or confidentiality (it's not encryption) — it proves integrity (the data hasn't changed).
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Option B is wrong — hashing is not encryption; it's one-way and doesn't protect confidentiality. Option C is wrong — a hash is not a timestamp; it's a content fingerprint. Option D is wrong — a hash proves data integrity, not the identity of the collector (that's a digital signature).

cards.question_text: A forensic investigator arrives at a crime scene where a suspect's laptop is powered on and logged in. The screen shows a VPN connection to an overseas server and a chat application with messages visible. What should the investigator do FIRST?
choices: Photograph the screen (including visible chat messages and VPN connection details), then capture RAM (which contains decrypted VPN keys, chat session data, and running processes), then proceed to disk imaging — following the order of volatility
Immediately pull the power cable to shut down the laptop and prevent remote data deletion
Close the chat application and disconnect the VPN to stop any ongoing communication
Start imaging the hard drive first since it contains the most persistent evidence
cards.answer: Photograph the screen (including visible chat messages and VPN connection details), then capture RAM (which contains decrypted VPN keys, chat session data, and running processes), then proceed to disk imaging — following the order of volatility
cards.explanation_correct: With a powered-on system, the investigator must follow the order of volatility. First: photograph the screen — it shows transient data (chat messages, VPN connection, open files) that will disappear on shutdown. Second: capture RAM — this is the highest-value volatile evidence. RAM contains: decrypted VPN session keys (the disk only has encrypted keys), active chat session data, running malware in memory, network connections, and decrypted files. Tools like FTK Imager, WinPMEM, or LiME (Linux) capture RAM to a file. Third: after RAM capture, proceed to disk imaging. Pulling the power (Option B) destroys all volatile evidence — RAM contents, network state, and running processes are lost forever, and the VPN/chat data vanishes.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Option B (pull power) is the worst mistake — it destroys RAM evidence, triggers potential anti-forensic scripts, and loses all transient data. Option C (close apps/VPN) alters the system state and destroys evidence — never interact with a suspect machine's applications. Option D (disk first) skips the most volatile evidence (RAM, screen) which will be lost by the time disk imaging completes.

cards.question_text: A forensic analyst needs to create a bit-for-bit copy of a 2TB hard drive for evidence. Which statement correctly describes best practices for forensic disk imaging?
choices: Use a write blocker (hardware or software) to prevent any writes to the original drive, image to a sterile target drive (pre-wiped and verified), compute hashes (MD5 + SHA-256) of the original and the image to verify they match, and document the entire process with timestamps
Use a standard USB cable to copy files from the original drive to a new drive using Windows Explorer, then hash the copied files
Boot the original computer from the evidence drive, then use a forensic tool to copy files selectively
Use dd to copy the drive, then securely erase the original drive immediately after imaging to prevent contamination
cards.answer: Use a write blocker (hardware or software) to prevent any writes to the original drive, image to a sterile target drive (pre-wiped and verified), compute hashes (MD5 + SHA-256) of the original and the image to verify they match, and document the entire process with timestamps
cards.explanation_correct: Forensic disk imaging must preserve the original evidence without alteration. A write blocker ensures no data (even automatic OS writes like mounting timestamps) is written to the original drive. The target drive must be sterile (wiped and verified with a hash showing all zeros) before imaging. The image is a bit-for-bit copy (including slack space, deleted files, and unallocated space — not just visible files). Hashing the original and the image with two algorithms proves they're identical. Documentation (who, what, when, where, how) maintains the chain of custody. Tools like FTK Imager, dd with a write blocker, or Tableau hardware imagers are standard. File copy (Option B) misses deleted files, slack space, and unallocated sectors.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Option B (file copy) is not forensic imaging — it only copies visible files, missing deleted data, slack space, and unallocated space where evidence often hides. Option C (boot from evidence drive) writes to the evidence drive (OS creates log files, updates timestamps) — it alters the original. Option D (erase original) destroys evidence — the original must be preserved for re-examination and court admissibility.

cards.question_text: An investigator analyzing a forensic disk image needs to recover deleted files and examine data in unallocated space. Which type of forensic analysis should they perform, and what data might they find?
choices: File carving and slack space analysis — they may find deleted files (whose data remains in unallocated clusters until overwritten), remnants in file slack (data between end of file and end of cluster), and fragments of previous file systems or browser artifacts in unallocated space
Password cracking — they should brute-force the user's password to unlock encrypted volumes
Network traffic analysis — they should reconstruct network packets from the disk image
Memory forensics — they should analyze the page file for RAM artifacts
cards.answer: File carving and slack space analysis — they may find deleted files (whose data remains in unallocated clusters until overwritten), remnants in file slack (data between end of file and end of cluster), and fragments of previous file systems or browser artifacts in unallocated space
cards.explanation_correct: When a file is deleted, the OS marks its clusters as available but doesn't erase the data — it remains until overwritten. File carving tools (like Autopsy, Foremost, Scalpel) scan unallocated space for file signatures (JPEG headers, PDF magic bytes, ZIP structures) and reconstruct files without relying on the file table. Slack space (file slack) contains data from the end of a file to the end of its last cluster — remnants of previous files that occupied that cluster. Unallocated space may contain deleted browser history, temporary files, previous file system remnants, and evidence the suspect tried to delete. This is why forensic imaging captures the entire disk (bit-for-bit), not just visible files — the invisible data is often the most valuable evidence.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Option B (password cracking) is a separate process — it may be necessary for encrypted volumes but isn't about recovering deleted files. Option C (network traffic from disk) is possible (pcap files) but isn't the primary method for deleted file recovery. Option D (page file analysis) is memory forensics, not disk forensics — the page file can contain RAM artifacts but that's a different analysis type.

cards.question_text: What is the chain of custody, and what must it document for each piece of evidence?
choices: A chronological record documenting who collected, handled, transported, stored, and accessed each piece of evidence, with timestamps, locations, hash values, and the purpose of each transfer — proving the evidence hasn't been altered from collection to court presentation
A physical chain (like a padlock chain) used to lock evidence storage rooms
A digital certificate that proves evidence is authentic
A chain of command showing who authorized the investigation
cards.answer: A chronological record documenting who collected, handled, transported, stored, and accessed each piece of evidence, with timestamps, locations, hash values, and the purpose of each transfer — proving the evidence hasn't been altered from collection to court presentation
cards.explanation_correct: Chain of custody is the legal documentation that proves evidence integrity from the moment it's collected to the moment it's presented in court. Each entry must record: (1) Who — name and role of person handling the evidence. (2) What — description of the evidence and its hash value. (3) When — date and time of collection/transfer. (4) Where — location where evidence was found and where it was stored. (5) Why — purpose of transfer (e.g., 'transported to forensic lab for imaging'). Any gap in the chain — an undocumented period where someone could have altered the evidence — can render the evidence inadmissible in court. The chain is typically a form (paper or digital) signed by each handler, with evidence stored in tamper-evident bags.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Option B is wrong — while physical chains/locks may be used, chain of custody is documentation, not hardware. Option C is wrong — it's a record, not a digital certificate. Option D is wrong — it's about evidence handling, not command authority.

cards.question_text: What is a tamper-evident seal/bag, and why is it used in forensic evidence collection?
choices: A sealed container (bag or tape with a unique serial number) that shows visible signs if someone has opened or tampered with it — providing physical proof that evidence hasn't been accessed between collection and lab analysis
A bag that destroys the evidence inside if someone tries to open it
A bag that encrypts the evidence so it can't be read without a password
A bag that blocks electromagnetic signals to prevent remote wiping of devices
cards.answer: A sealed container (bag or tape with a unique serial number) that shows visible signs if someone has opened or tampered with it — providing physical proof that evidence hasn't been accessed between collection and lab analysis
cards.explanation_correct: Tamper-evident bags (also called evidence bags) have serialized seals that break visibly if opened. Once sealed, the bag shows a VOID pattern or torn seal if tampered with. The serial number is recorded in the chain of custody. When the evidence reaches the lab, the analyst verifies the seal is intact before opening — if the seal is broken, the chain of custody is compromised and the evidence may be inadmissible. Tamper-evident tape works similarly on larger items. Faraday bags (Option D) are different — they block electromagnetic signals to prevent remote wiping of phones/laptops, but they're about signal isolation, not tamper evidence. Both are used together: a device goes in a Faraday bag, which is then sealed in a tamper-evident bag.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Option B is wrong — tamper-evident bags don't destroy evidence; they reveal tampering. Option C is wrong — they don't encrypt; they provide physical tamper detection. Option D describes a Faraday bag, which is a different tool (signal blocking, not tamper evidence).

cards.question_text: During a court proceeding, the defense attorney challenges a hard drive image, stating there was a 3-hour gap in the chain of custody log between when the evidence was collected and when it was logged into the evidence locker. What is the likely consequence?
choices: The evidence may be ruled inadmissible — the undocumented 3-hour gap means the prosecution cannot prove the drive wasn't accessed, modified, or swapped during that period, breaking the integrity guarantee that chain of custody provides
Nothing — a 3-hour gap is within the acceptable tolerance for evidence handling
The evidence is still admissible but the forensic analyst must re-hash the drive in court
The judge will automatically convict the investigator of evidence tampering
cards.answer: The evidence may be ruled inadmissible — the undocumented 3-hour gap means the prosecution cannot prove the drive wasn't accessed, modified, or swapped during that period, breaking the integrity guarantee that chain of custody provides
cards.explanation_correct: Chain of custody must be continuous and unbroken. A gap — even a short one — creates reasonable doubt about evidence integrity. The defense will argue: 'During those 3 hours, someone could have modified the image, planted evidence, or swapped the drive.' The prosecution cannot prove otherwise because there's no documentation. Judges take this seriously — if the chain is broken, the evidence may be excluded entirely (the legal standard varies by jurisdiction, but inadmissibility is the risk). This is why every transfer, no matter how brief, must be documented: '14:00 — Evidence collected by Investigator A at suspect's office. 14:05 — Transported to vehicle. 14:30 — Arrived at evidence locker. 14:35 — Logged in by Evidence Custodian B.' No gaps.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Option B is wrong — there is no 'acceptable tolerance' for gaps in chain of custody; any undocumented period is a break. Option C is wrong — re-hashing in court proves the current state matches but doesn't prove the gap period didn't include tampering. Option D is wrong — a gap suggests negligence, not necessarily criminal tampering by the investigator.

cards.question_text: A compromised web server is actively exfiltrating data to a C2 server. The IR team has three options: (A) pull the network cable, (B) isolate via VLAN change, (C) shut down the server. Which is the best containment strategy and why?
choices: Isolate via VLAN change — it cuts off C2 communication while keeping the server powered on, preserving volatile evidence (RAM, running processes, network connections) for forensic analysis and allowing monitoring of the attacker's persistence attempts
Pull the network cable — it's the fastest and most direct way to stop exfiltration
Shut down the server — it immediately stops all malicious activity and is the safest option
Do nothing and let the attacker continue — monitoring their activity provides intelligence
cards.answer: Isolate via VLAN change — it cuts off C2 communication while keeping the server powered on, preserving volatile evidence (RAM, running processes, network connections) for forensic analysis and allowing monitoring of the attacker's persistence attempts
cards.explanation_correct: VLAN isolation is the gold standard for network containment of a compromised server. It achieves: (1) Stops C2 communication — the server can't reach the attacker or exfiltrate data. (2) Preserves volatile evidence — the server stays on, so RAM (containing decrypted data, running malware, C2 keys) is intact for forensic capture. (3) Allows monitoring — the IR team can observe if the attacker has persistence mechanisms (scheduled tasks, new services) that try to reconnect. (4) Maintains business context — the server's state is preserved for root-cause analysis. Pulling the cable (Option A) works but is less elegant — it's physical and doesn't allow network-level monitoring of reconnection attempts. Shutting down (Option C) destroys volatile evidence. Option D (do nothing) is unacceptable — active exfiltration must be contained.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Option A (pull cable) works but is less useful than VLAN isolation — no network telemetry, and physical access is needed. Option C (shutdown) destroys RAM evidence and may trigger anti-forensic cleanup. Option D (let it run) is only acceptable in rare 'watch and learn' scenarios with senior approval — active data exfiltration must be contained.

cards.question_text: After eradicating a malware infection from a network of 200 endpoints, the IR team moves to the recovery phase. What are the key activities in recovery, and what critical check must be performed before returning systems to production?
choices: Restore systems from known-clean backups or rebuild from gold images, apply all security patches, verify system integrity (compare to hardened baseline), monitor for re-infection indicators, and confirm the original vulnerability is patched before returning to production
Simply turn the systems back on and let users resume work — eradication means the threat is gone
Reformat all hard drives and reinstall the OS, then immediately return to production without testing
Purchase new hardware for all 200 endpoints — compromised machines can never be trusted again
cards.answer: Restore systems from known-clean backups or rebuild from gold images, apply all security patches, verify system integrity (compare to hardened baseline), monitor for re-infection indicators, and confirm the original vulnerability is patched before returning to production
cards.explanation_correct: Recovery is about safely returning systems to normal operation. Key steps: (1) Restore from clean backups or rebuild from gold/master images — don't trust the compromised system state. (2) Apply all patches and hardening before reconnecting to the network. (3) Verify integrity — compare the rebuilt system to the hardened baseline (CIS Benchmarks); ensure no backdoors remain. (4) Confirm the original vulnerability that enabled the breach is fixed — if it isn't, the same attack will recur. (5) Phase the return — bring systems back in monitored stages, watching for IoCs. (6) Enhanced monitoring — heightened SIEM/EDR alerts for 2-4 weeks post-recovery to catch re-infection early. Recovery without patching the root cause guarantees recurrence.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Option B is dangerously wrong — 'eradication complete' doesn't mean systems are safe to use; they may still have backdoors or unpatched vulnerabilities. Option C is partially right (rebuilding) but wrong to skip integrity verification and patching before returning to production. Option D is overkill — most systems can be rebuilt from clean images; replacing hardware is unnecessary unless physically compromised.

cards.question_text: Two weeks after a major ransomware incident was contained and systems were recovered, the IR team holds a post-incident review (lessons learned) meeting. Which of the following is the most valuable outcome of this meeting?
choices: Actionable improvements to detection, response procedures, and security controls — identifying what worked, what failed, and specific changes (new SIEM rules, faster escalation paths, additional training) with assigned owners and deadlines to prevent or improve response to the next incident
A formal report to blame the individuals who failed to detect the initial intrusion and recommend disciplinary action
A document confirming that the incident is fully resolved and no further investigation is needed
A marketing statement declaring the organization's security is now impenetrable
cards.answer: Actionable improvements to detection, response procedures, and security controls — identifying what worked, what failed, and specific changes (new SIEM rules, faster escalation paths, additional training) with assigned owners and deadlines to prevent or improve response to the next incident
cards.explanation_correct: The post-incident activity phase (NIST's 4th phase) is where organizations learn from the incident. A blameless post-mortem focuses on systems and processes, not individuals. Key outcomes: (1) What worked well — e.g., EDR detected the ransomware in 5 minutes. (2) What failed — e.g., SIEM alert for lateral movement was ignored for 2 hours due to alert fatigue. (3) Action items with owners and deadlines — e.g., 'Tune SIEM rules to reduce false positives (SOC lead, 2 weeks),' 'Add MFA to all VPN accounts (IT lead, 1 month),' 'Run quarterly tabletop exercises (IR lead, ongoing).' (4) Update IR playbooks with lessons learned. (5) Share findings (sanitized) with broader teams. Without this phase, the same vulnerabilities and response gaps will persist.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Option B is wrong — blame culture destroys trust and makes people hide incidents; blameless post-mortems focus on systemic improvements. Option C is wrong — the review isn't about closing the case; it's about learning and improving. Option D is dangerously wrong — no security is 'impenetrable,' and claiming so is both false and legally risky.
